title: Troubleshooting
text: Some R packages have to be compiled when you install them. If install.packages() fails with errors about compilers, make, gfortran, or missing files like cmath, follow the steps for your computer below.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Windows users – installing Rtools (required for compiling R packages)
text:
Windows users – installing Rtools (required for compiling R packages)
Some R packages are available only as source code. On Windows you need Rtools (a collection of compilers and build utilities) so that R can install those packages. macOS and Linux already ship suitable build tools; Windows does not.

Do I already have Rtools?

In a fresh R session (the Positron Console) run:
Sys.which("make")

If you get a blank result (““), R cannot find make ⇒ Rtools is missing. • If you see a full path containing rtools….exe, you’re all set! NO NEED TO GO ANY FURTHER!


Find the Rtools version that matches your R

Check your R version:
R.version.string

Your R version Install this Rtools 4.5.x Rtools45 4.4.x Rtools44 4.3.x Rtools43 4.2.x Rtools42 (no longer needed if you upgraded R)


Download Rtools


Go to https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/ Click the folder for your version (e.g. rtools43 for 4.3; rtools44 for 4.4; rtools45 for 4.5). Download the .exe installer (≈ 200 MB).


Install Rtools


Close Positron (or RStudio). Run the downloaded installer. When prompted, tick “Add Rtools to system PATH.” Accept the default install path (C:, C:, …). Finish the installation (it may take a minute).


Verify the installation


After installation open a new R session (or reboot) and run:

Sys.which("make")
#>                  make 
#> "C:\\rtools45\\usr\\bin\\make.exe"   # or rtools44 / rtools43

title: Troubleshooting
section: Mac users – installing gfortran and Xcode Command Line Tools (required for compiling R packages)
text:
Mac users – installing gfortran and Xcode Command Line Tools (required for compiling R packages)

macOS users – installing gfortran (required for compiling R packages)
Some R packages require a Fortran compiler to install from source.
macOS does not include one by default.
You need to install gfortran manually and the version must match your R version.


Do I already have gfortran?

In a fresh R session (the Positron Console) run:
Sys.which("gfortran") 

If you get a blank result (““), gfortran is missing ⇒ you need to install it.
If you see a path like /opt/gfortran/bin/gfortran, you’re all set! NO NEED TO GO ANY FURTHER!


Find the gfortran version that matches your R Check your R version:


Look at the top of the R console window OR
copy/paste this into your terminal

R.version.string 

If your R version is 4.5.x Install gfortran
If your R version is 4.3 to 4.4.x install gfortran 12.2
If you R version is older then no need to install gfortran


Download gfortran


https://mac.r-project.org/tools/gfortran-12.2-universal.pkg
https://mac.r-project.org/tools/gfortran-14.2-universal.pkg


Install gfortran


Close Positron (or RStudio).
Double-click the downloaded .pkg file.
Follow the installer prompts and accept the default install path. Enter your Mac password when prompted. Finish the installation.


Verify the installation After installation open a new R session and run:

Sys.which("gfortran") 
#\> gfortran 
#\> "/opt/gfortran/bin/gfortran" 

If you see the path above, gfortran is installed correctly ✅
If you still get a blank result, try restarting your Mac and running again.


One more check - verify R and gfortran are in sync


Run this in R:

system("gfortran --version") 
You should see output like:
GNU Fortran (GCC) 14.2.0 # if you are on R 4.5 
GNU Fortran (GCC) 12.2.0 # if you are on R 4.4 or 4.3 

If the version number does not match your R version, you have the wrong gfortran installed and need to download the correct version from https://mac.r-project.org/tools/
macOS users – fixing missing C++ header files (required for compiling R packages)

If you see errors like these when installing packages:
fatal error: 'cmath' file not found 
fatal error: 'cstdlib' file not 
found fatal error: 'cstring' file not found 
This means your Xcode Command Line Tools are missing or out of date. This is common after a macOS upgrade.

Do I have this problem?

In R run:
system("xcode-select -p")

If you get an error or a blank result ⇒ Command Line Tools are missing. • If you see /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools ⇒ they are installed. NO NEED TO GO ANY FURTHER!


Fix the problem Close Positron (or RStudio) completely. Open the Mac Terminal application and run these commands one at a time:


Step 1 - Remove the old Command Line Tools:
sudo rm -rf /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools 

You will be prompted for your Mac password.
Type it and press Enter (you will not see the password as you type - this is normal).



Step 2 - Reinstall the Command Line Tools:
xcode-select --install 

A popup window will appear.
Click Install and wait for it to finish.
This may take 5 to 10 minutes depending on your internet connection



Step 3 - Verify the installation was successful:
xcode-select -p 

You should see:

/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools

Try installing your packages again


Once the Command Line Tools are installed, reopen Positron and re-run the install.packages() line in Part 2 of the Session 1 student script.



⚠️ Note for macOS beta users:
If you are running a beta version of macOS, package compilation errors are more likely because R and its tools may not yet be fully compatible with the newest macOS releases. If you continue to have problems after reinstalling the Command Line Tools, the most reliable solution is to use the stable (non-beta) release of macOS.


🔑 Quick Reference Card
Your Setup R Version Need
Windows 4.5.x = Rtools45
Windows 4.4.x = Rtools44
Windows 4.3.x = Rtools43
Mac 4.5.x = gfortran 14.2
Mac 4.4.x or 4.3.x = gfortran 12.2
Mac (any version) = any Xcode Command Line Tools

title: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets
text:
Order the bars
Alphabetical order rarely helps. fct_infreq() orders by count (most common first), and fct_rev() flips it so the longest bar is at the top:

ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(hospital_name)))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Cases by hospital", x = "Number of cases", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()








y = NULL removes an axis title the reader doesn’t need.
crumbs: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets

title: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets
text:
Fill by a second variable
Map fill to split each bar. The position argument controls how the pieces are arranged:

# "stack" (the default): counts, stacked
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack")









# "fill": every bar is 100% — compares PROPORTIONS across groups
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")









# "dodge": side by side — compares COUNTS within each group
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")














Note🤔 Think about it: which version answers “do older patients die more often?”





The 100% "fill" version. The stacked version mostly shows that there are many more young patients than old ones, so the small bars for older groups are hard to compare.









Important✏️ TRY IT (3 min): cases by district



Make a horizontal bar chart of measles cases by district, longest bar on top.
✅ Check: North is at the top; Unknown is at the bottom






NoteShow solution






ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(district)))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Measles cases by district", x = "Number of cases", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()








fct_infreq() puts North (342 cases) first, and fct_rev() moves it to the top. Unknown (34 cases) ends up at the bottom.
crumbs: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets

title: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets
text:
Rotate long labels
If you keep labels on the x-axis, rotate them so they don’t overlap:

ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = hospital_name)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))














Important✏️ TRY IT (4 min): vaccination by age group



Make a 100% bar chart of vaccinated by age_cat, with vacc_colors, a percent y-axis, labels, and theme_minimal().
✅ Check: every bar reaches 100%; “Yes” is blue in every bar






NoteShow solution






ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill", color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vacc_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Vaccination status of measles cases by age group",
    x     = "Age group",
    y     = "Percent of cases",
    fill  = "Vaccinated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








position = "fill" makes every bar 100%, and because vacc_colors is a named vector, “Yes” is always blue, “No” orange, and “Unknown” gray.

title: Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets
text:
Epicurve by outcome

linelist %>%
  filter(onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01")) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = onset_date, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = outcome_colors) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  labs(x = "Week of onset", y = "Number of cases", fill = "Outcome") +
  theme_minimal()














Important✏️ TRY IT (5 min): the measles epicurve



Make a weekly epicurve of measles report_date, filled by vaccinated, with vacc_colors and scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b"). Save it as measles_epicurve — you will need it in Part 7. Hint: filter(!is.na(report_date)) first. When did the outbreak peak?
✅ Check: the peak is in the second half of March (about 115 cases in one week)






NoteShow solution






measles_epicurve <- measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(report_date)) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = report_date, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vacc_colors) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(
    title = "Measles cases by week of report, 2024",
    x     = "Week of report",
    y     = "Number of cases",
    fill  = "Vaccinated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

measles_epicurve








The outbreak peaked in the second half of March 2024, with 117 cases in the peak week. Saving the plot as an object means it only appears when you print it (the last line).

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
Percentages
count() makes a column called n. Divide by the total to get a proportion, and use scales::percent() to show it nicely:

linelist %>%
  count(outcome) %>%
  mutate(percent = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1))

  outcome    n percent
1 Recover 2158   33.5%
2   Death 2840   44.0%
3 Unknown 1453   22.5%

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
Percentages within groups: group_by()
group_by() makes the next steps happen separately for each group. Here, sum(n) becomes the total within each age group, so each age group adds up to 100%:

linelist %>%
  group_by(age_cat) %>%
  count(outcome) %>%
  mutate(percent = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) %>%
  ungroup()

# A tibble: 24 × 4
   age_cat  outcome     n percent
   <fct>    <fct>   <int> <chr>  
 1 Under 18 Recover  1322 33.4%  
 2 Under 18 Death    1755 44.3%  
 3 Under 18 Unknown   885 22.3%  
 4 18-29    Recover   498 34.2%  
 5 18-29    Death     648 44.5%  
 6 18-29    Unknown   309 21.2%  
 7 30-39    Recover   179 30.8%  
 8 30-39    Death     256 44.0%  
 9 30-39    Unknown   147 25.3%  
10 40-49    Recover    85 34.7%  
# ℹ 14 more rows








Note🤔 Think about it: how is this different from count(age_cat, outcome) without group_by()?





Without grouping, the percentages are out of all 6,451 cases, so all the rows together add up to 100%. With group_by(age_cat), each age group adds up to 100% on its own.









Tipungroup() when you’re done



A grouped data frame stays grouped. End with ungroup() so later steps don’t surprise you.

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
By group
Add group_by() first to get one row per group:

linelist %>%
  group_by(outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    mean_age   = mean(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_age = median(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bmi   = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_temp  = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  outcome     n mean_age median_age mean_bmi mean_temp
  <fct>   <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Recover  2158     16.1         13     30.6      38.6
2 Death    2840     15.9         13     30.7      38.6
3 Unknown  1453     16.2         14     30.4      38.6








NoteUseful summary functions



Centre: mean(), median() · Spread: sd(), IQR(), min(), max(), quantile(x, 0.25) · Counts: n(), n_distinct(), sum(is.na(x))

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
section: The same calculation on many columns: across()
text:
The same calculation on many columns: across()
You met across() in Session 3. In summarise() it saves a lot of typing:

linelist %>%
  group_by(outcome) %>%
  summarise(across(c(age_years, bmi, temp), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  outcome age_years   bmi  temp
  <fct>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Recover      16.1  30.6  38.6
2 Death        15.9  30.7  38.6
3 Unknown      16.2  30.4  38.6

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
Percentages of “yes”
fever == "yes" is TRUE or FALSE for each row (vectorization, from Session 4). sum() counts the TRUEs, and mean() gives the proportion that are TRUE:

linelist %>%
  group_by(outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    n_cases   = n(),
    n_fever   = sum(fever == "yes"),
    pct_fever = round(mean(fever == "yes") * 100, 1),
    pct_cough = round(mean(cough == "yes") * 100, 1),
    pct_vomit = round(mean(vomit == "yes") * 100, 1)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  outcome n_cases n_fever pct_fever pct_cough pct_vomit
  <fct>     <int>   <int>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Recover    2158    1708      79.1      82        47.9
2 Death      2840    2245      79        82.9      48.8
3 Unknown    1453    1124      77.4      84.2      46.5








TipSave summaries as objects



Every result here is a data frame. Save it with <- and you can plot it (Sessions 6 and 7), join it, or export it like any other data.








Important✏️ TRY IT (4 min): statistics by outcome



For each measles outcome, calculate the number of cases, mean and median age, mean temperature, and mean days in hospital (careful: NAs!).
✅ Check: Recovered n = 1048, median age 7; Died n = 50, median age 5






NoteShow solution






measles %>%
  group_by(outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    mean_age   = mean(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_age = median(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_temp  = mean(temp_c),
    mean_days  = mean(days_in_hospital, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  outcome       n mean_age median_age mean_temp mean_days
  <fct>     <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Recovered  1048     8.92          7      38.8      4.94
2 Died         50     6.80          5      38.8      4.55
3 Unknown      65     7.47          5      38.7      5.12


Children who died were younger than children who recovered (median age 5 vs 7). days_in_hospital is missing for patients who were never hospitalized, so it needs na.rm = TRUE.











Important✏️ TRY IT (4 min): case rates by district



Calculate cases per 10,000 people by district (number of cases / population * 10000), sorted highest first.
Hint: count(district, population) gives both columns; then mutate() and arrange(desc()).
✅ Check: East has the highest rate (22.8); Central the lowest (5.2)






NoteShow solution






measles %>%
  count(district, population) %>%
  mutate(rate_per_10k = round(n / population * 10000, 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(rate_per_10k))

  district population   n rate_per_10k
1     East      98000 223         22.8
2     West      76500 170         22.2
3    South     142000 284         20.0
4    North     185000 342         18.5
5  Central     210000 110          5.2
6  Unknown         NA  34           NA


Central has the most people but the lowest rate: raw counts and rates can tell different stories. The “Unknown” district has no population, so it gets no rate.

title: Session 5: Summarizing Your Data
text:
Save it to Word
as_flex_table() turns the table into a flextable, and save_as_docx() writes the Word file. The new file appears in the outputs/ folder in the Explorer.

table1 %>%
  as_flex_table() %>%

title: Session 3: Missing Data, Joins, and Export
text:
How joins work
A join combines two data frames by matching rows on a key column that both share. A tiny example first:

patients <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3), name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cho"))
labs     <- tibble(id = c(2, 3, 4), result = c("positive", "negative", "positive"))

left_join(patients, labs, by = "id")    # all patients; NA where no lab result

# A tibble: 3 × 3
     id name  result  
  <dbl> <chr> <chr>   
1     1 Ana   <NA>    
2     2 Ben   positive
3     3 Cho   negative

inner_join(patients, labs, by = "id")   # only ids in BOTH

# A tibble: 2 × 3
     id name  result  
  <dbl> <chr> <chr>   
1     2 Ben   positive
2     3 Cho   negative

full_join(patients, labs, by = "id")    # everyone from both

# A tibble: 4 × 3
     id name  result  
  <dbl> <chr> <chr>   
1     1 Ana   <NA>    
2     2 Ben   positive
3     3 Cho   negative
4     4 <NA>  positive

anti_join(patients, labs, by = "id")    # patients with NO lab result

# A tibble: 1 × 2
     id name 
  <dbl> <chr>
1     1 Ana  









Join
Keeps




left_join()
every row of the first data frame


right_join()
every row of the second data frame


inner_join()
only rows that match in both


full_join()
every row from both


anti_join()
rows of the first with no match — great for checking



left_join() is the one you will use most: start with your main dataset and add information to it.

import() + here()
rio::import() reads almost any file type (.csv, .xlsx, .txt, SPSS, Stata, SAS, …). It works out the type from the file extension, so you only need to learn one function. Save the result with <-, or it only prints to the Console and is gone.

hosp_info <- import(here("raw_data", "hosp_info.txt"))   # tab-separated text

File names must match exactly, including capitals and the extension.
“Error: No such file” means the folder or file name is misspelled, or the workshop folder isn’t open (check the Explorer on the left).

Base R: read.csv() — older, slower, and needs more settings
readr: read_csv() — the tidyverse version, fast and returns a tibble
haven: read_sav(), read_dta(), read_sas() — SPSS, Stata, SAS files

title: Instructor notes: Session 7
text:
Teaching notes by part
Part 1 — Set up. Same import pipeline as Session 6. Point out why we save vacc_colors now: every plot later in the session reuses it, so “Yes” is always the same blue.
Part 2 — geom_bar(). Start with x = hospital_name so learners see the overlapping labels, then switch to y. Ask the class: which version (stack, fill, or dodge) answers “do older patients die more often?” — the 100% "fill" version; the stacked one mostly shows that there are many more young patients.
Part 3 — geom_col(). Ask the class: the 70–79 and 80+ bars are based on very few patients — check n in death_by_age. How much should we trust them? — Not much: 70–79 has 6 patients and 80+ has 1 (0% died).
Part 4 — Choosing colors. The original workshop used red/green and dark red/red. These pages use blue, orange, and gray (#2a78d6, #eb6834, #9a9a95); blue, orange, and aqua (#2a78d6, #eb6834, #1baf7a) stay distinguishable for the common types of color blindness. For more colors, the viridis scales are built in: scale_fill_viridis_d().
Part 5 — Epidemic curves. Show the full-range epicurve first and ask the class: what is going on before 2014? — 538 onset dates fall in 2012–2013 (April 2012 – April 2013), long before the outbreak, and every one belongs to a case ID that appears more than once (the duplicate IDs from Session 3), usually with the same day and month but a different year. Almost certainly data-entry errors. Make the point: plots reveal problems tables hide.
Part 6 — Facets. Point out that facets share axes by default, which is what makes them comparable; scales = "free_y" breaks that. In the TRY IT, district peaks are close but not identical with weekly bins (Central and North peak the week of 17 March, East the week of 24 March, West 10 March, and South is nearly flat from early March into April) — “they all peak in March” is the fair answer.
Part 7 — Saving plots. Have learners open the saved PNG from the Explorer (outputs/ folder) — text size in the file often looks different from the Plots pane; adjust width/height to fix it.
Wrap-up. Recap the journey: problem list (S1) → cleaning pipeline (S2) → de-duplicated, joined file (S3) → vectors, subsetting, reshaping (S4) → summary tables and Table 1 (S5) → histograms, scatter, box plots (S6) → bar charts, epicurves, facets saved to files (S7). Session 8 (Programming) is optional: functions, if/else, and loops — for example, one epicurve per hospital automatically. Encourage learners to repeat the whole workflow on their own data.

title: Instructor notes: Session 5
text:
Teaching notes by part
Overview — why these three packages. There are many packages for summary tables (base R summary() and table(), psych::describe(), rstatix::get_summary_stats(), …). This session teaches three that cover almost every need: dplyr (count()/summarise()) for flexible summaries you can plot, janitor (tabyl()) for quick cross-tabs, and gtsummary for tables you publish. Say this up front if learners ask “why not X?”.
Part 1 — Set up. Remind learners this is the dataset finished in Session 3: cleaned, de-duplicated, and joined to the case information (symptoms and temperature). They can confirm the import in the Variables pane.
Part 2 — Factors. Run count(age_cat) before relevelling and ask learners what’s wrong with the order (“Under 18” sorts after “80+”). Emphasize that the order carries through to plots too — they’ll see it again in Sessions 6 and 7. Note: the .rds files saved in Session 3 contain plain text columns, not factors, so the order has to be set again after every import (the student script says this; the original instructor script implied the .rds already kept the order). A misspelled level gives an “Unknown levels” warning and is silently ignored.
Part 3 — Counting and percentages. After the group_by(age_cat) %>% count(outcome) example, ask the class:

How is this different from count(age_cat, outcome) without group_by()? — Without grouping, the percentages are out of all 6,451 cases, so all rows together add up to 100%. With grouping, each age group adds up to 100%.

Stress ungroup(): a grouped data frame stays grouped and can surprise them later.
Part 4 — summarise(). Show what happens without na.rm = TRUE (the whole result becomes NA). Connect mean(fever == "yes") to Session 4’s vectorization: TRUE/FALSE, sum() counts the TRUEs, mean() gives the proportion. In the “statistics by outcome” TRY IT, days_in_hospital needs na.rm = TRUE because non-hospitalized patients have NA. In the district rates TRY IT, point out that Central has the most people but the lowest rate — counts and rates tell different stories — and that the “Unknown” district gets no rate.
Part 5 — tabyl(). Spend a moment on the order of the adorn_ functions — totals must come before percentages because they need the raw counts. The vaccination-and-death TRY IT (6.3% vs 0.7%) is a good moment to discuss what this data does and doesn’t show: it’s fictional practice data, the numbers of deaths are small (2 vaccinated deaths), and a crude cross-tab doesn’t adjust for anything (e.g. age).
Part 6 — Table 1. Explain why we turn “Unknown” back into NA with na_if(): in Session 3 we replaced NA with “Unknown” so missing values show up in counts, but tbl_summary() has its own Missing row. na_if() with where(is.character) only touches text columns, so factor columns (age_cat, vaccinated) keep “Unknown” as a category. Mention add_p() but only for analyses where a statistical test is planned. The Word export uses as_flex_table() %>% flextable::save_as_docx(); have learners find outputs/table1.docx in the Explorer and open it. For the measles Table 1, point out that “Missing” days in hospital means not hospitalized, not lost data.
Wrap-up. Recap: fct_relevel(), count(), group_by(), summarise(), across(), tabyl() + adorn_*(), tbl_summary(). Preview Session 6 — Plotting basics: ggplot2 from the ground up — histograms, scatter plots, and box plots.

Teaching notes by part
Part 1 — Set up. Explain trust = TRUE briefly (an .rds can contain R code; we made these files ourselves). If a learner’s measles_clean.rds is missing or broken, they can download a fresh copy from GitHub.
Part 2 — Where is data missing? Ask the class: is every missing value a mistake? — No. date_of_outcome is missing for patients with no outcome yet (real information); bmi is missing where Session 2 set impossible values to NA; a missing case_id is a problem because those rows can’t be linked. Point out that drop_na(bmi) would lose 1382 of 6604 patients.
Part 3 — Rows with no ID. Build paste0("ID", sprintf("%05d", row_number())) up piece by piece in the Console (row_number(), then sprintf("%05d", 1), then paste0()) if learners look lost.
Part 4 — Duplicates. After distinct(), get_dupes(case_id) still finds 1106 rows whose ID appears more than once. These rows are not exact copies, so distinct() keeps them. In a real project you would ask the data owner which record is correct. We keep them for this workshop, but it’s a good discussion point: cleaning often needs people, not just code.
Part 5 — Replacing missing values. Point out that where(is.character) skips number and date columns, so they keep their NAs — which is what we want.
Part 6 — Joining datasets. Draw the tiny patients/labs example on the board if you can. The old version of this workshop ran distinct() after the join. Removing duplicates before joining (Part 4) is the better habit: duplicates are easier to spot in the original data, and they can’t multiply during the join. Stress the row-count check: 6451 rows before and after.
Part 7 — Exporting: live demo of the .csv problem. Save linelist_clean as a .csv, read it back, and look for the missing IDs:
export(linelist_clean, here("processed_data", "test.csv"))
import(here("processed_data", "test.csv")) %>% filter(is.na(case_id)) %>% nrow()   # 0, not 130!
The 130 missing IDs came back as blank text "", so is.na() no longer finds them. This is why Session 2 saved linelist_clean as .rds. Delete test.csv afterwards.
Make sure everyone saves measles_final.rds — they need it for every remaining session. Early finishers: ⭐ Bonus (inner vs left join).
Wrap-up. Today: is.na(), drop_na(), filter(!is.na()), distinct(), get_dupes(), replace_na(), across(), select(), joins, export(). The data are ready! Sessions 4–8 start from combined_linelist.rds and measles_final.rds. Preview Session 4 — Data structures: vectors, base R subsetting, and pivot_longer() / pivot_wider().

The teaching rhythm
Every part of every lesson follows the same three steps:

👀 Follow along — you live-code the new skill on the workshop dataset (the outbreak linelist). Learners type the same code into their student script.
✏️ TRY IT — learners immediately do the same thing on the practice dataset (the measles outbreak). Each TRY IT takes 1–10 minutes and has a ✅ Check so learners know they got it right.

title: Instructor Guide

Live coding tips

Type, don’t paste. Learners need to see code being written — and your typos and fixes are useful teaching moments.
Go slower than feels natural, and say what you’re typing as you type it.
Use a big font (Positron: View → Appearance → Zoom In, or Cmd/Ctrl + +) and a light color theme for the projector.
Run every line and talk about the output before moving on.
Read errors out loud and fix them together — learners will meet the same errors.

title: Instructor notes: Session 2
text:
Teaching notes by part
Overall rhythm. Learners build two cleaned datasets side by side: linelist_clean with you (Follow along), and measles_clean in the TRY ITs. Both are built one step at a time: each part takes the current object, adds one fix, and saves it back with <-. Part 7 then shows the same linelist steps as one pipeline — the version you would keep in a real project. If a learner’s object gets into a bad state, they can re-run from Part 2 (linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>% clean_names()). The filled-in script is solutions/Session 2 - Cleaning_SOLUTIONS.R.
Part 1 — Set up. Briefly put up the Session 1 problem list and the “Fixed in” column; emphasize never edit the raw data file.
Part 2 — Column names. Show names() before and after clean_names(). Point out that backticks are no longer needed. Stress that in rename() the new name goes on the left.
Part 3 — Types. Point out the “NAs introduced by coercion” warning when learners convert measles age_years: it is expected (the 27 “unknown” values) — a warning is not an error. The TRY IT’s summary() showing a max of 999 sets up Part 4. A common slip is forgetting the <-, so nothing is saved.
Part 4 — if_else(). Ask the class (a “Think about it” on the lesson page):

What would have happened in later analyses if we had skipped the months → years step? — A 6-month-old baby would be counted as 6 years old (37 ages are in months).

Explain why we replace impossible weights with NA rather than deleting the row: we keep the patient’s age, outcome, and dates.
Part 5 — case_when(). Point out that rows matching no condition become NA (gender), and that .default catches everything else (hospital). Show count(hospital, hospital_name) as the way to check every recode. Common errors: = instead of ~, a missing or extra comma. The district TRY IT is the hardest of the session — expect red sticky notes; a hint is to run str_to_title() first so each str_detect() only needs to catch misspellings.
Part 6 — New variables. Ask the class (a “Think about it” on the lesson page):

A BMI of 1,250? — The heights and weights don’t fit together. Set BMIs outside 10–60 to NA.

About 1,400 BMIs (1,382) end up NA because the height and weight values in this teaching dataset are unrealistic. The old version of this workshop filtered out those rows, which removed about 20% of the cases from every later analysis. Setting only the bad value to NA keeps everything else about the patient.
For age_cat, point out that case_when() stops at the first TRUE line, and warn against ending with TRUE ~ "80+" / .default = "80+" — it puts missing ages into the oldest group. count() shows the groups in alphabetical order; that is fixed with factors in Session 4.
Part 7 — One pipeline and saving. Point out that inside one mutate(), later lines can use columns made on earlier lines (bmi is created, then fixed). Make sure everyone saves measles_clean.rds — they need it in Session 3. Early finishers: the ⭐ Bonus asks them to rewrite all their measles steps as one pipeline.
Wrap-up. Today: clean_names(), rename(), mutate(), as.Date(), as.numeric(), if_else(), case_when(), str_detect(), export(). Preview Session 3 — Missing data, joins, and export: rows with no Case ID, duplicates, replacing missing values, joining case_info, and saving the final datasets.

title: Instructor notes: Session 4
text:
Teaching notes by part
Why this session matters. Sessions 1–3 used tidyverse functions that hide how R stores data. This session opens the hood. Vectors and vectorization explain why mutate() works on a whole column at once; base-R subsetting is everywhere in other people’s code, help pages, and Stack Overflow answers, and learners need it to write functions in Session 8; and reshaping is needed for many summaries and plots.
Part 2 — Vectors and types. Point out that c(1, 2, "unknown") is exactly why one “unknown” turned the whole age column into text in Session 1. Show that ages and the other objects appear in the Variables pane, which also shows each vector’s type and length.
Part 3 — Vectorization. Stress that mutate() is just a vectorized calculation on a column — no loop needed. Point out that sum()/mean() of a comparison counts/gives proportions; they will use mean(fever == "yes") * 100 inside summarise() in Session 5.
Part 4 — Subsetting with base R. Rows first, then columns — have learners say it out loud. A common slip is forgetting the comma (df[1:3] picks columns). Spend time on the NA warning box: nrow(linelist[linelist$temp > 40, ]) gives 244, nrow(filter(linelist, temp > 40)) gives 93 — base R adds a row of NAs for each of the 151 missing temperatures. The Part 4 TRY IT (c) repeats this trap on the measles data (225 vs 196, 29 missing ages), so let learners discover it before you explain.
Part 5 — Tidy data and pivot_longer(). Point out that “observation” depends on the question: wide symptoms are fine for one symptom at a time, but long format lets one count() handle all five. nrow(symptoms_long) is 32255 = 6451 patients × 5 symptoms. The plot is a preview of Session 6 — don’t explain ggplot yet.
Part 6 — pivot_wider(). Emphasize the rule of thumb: long for R, wide for people. Mention values_fill = 0 (the hospital × outcome table has no empty combinations, so it isn’t needed here).
Wrap-up. Today: vectors and types, c(), class(), vectorized maths and comparisons, sum()/mean() of TRUE/FALSE, [ ], $, [[ ]], tidy data, pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(). Next is Session 5 (Summarizing: count(), group_by() + summarise(), tabyl(), Table 1); Session 8 returns to vectors and subsetting when writing functions and loops.

Teaching notes by part
Every part. Build each plot one layer at a time and run it after every +, so learners see what each layer adds.
Part 1 — Set up. Point out that the factor order from Session 5 isn’t saved in the .rds file, so it has to be set again right after importing — and that import() and mutate() can go in one pipeline.
Part 2 — The grammar of graphics. Run the three steps separately: empty canvas, axes only, then bars. Stress + not %>% between layers, and that + goes at the end of the line — the two most common beginner errors.
Part 3 — Histograms. Point out the “using bins = 30” message from the Part 2 plot, then choose binwidth yourself. Live-try binwidth = 1 and binwidth = 10 so learners see the shape change. In the TRY IT, reassure learners that the “removed rows” warning is just the 29 missing ages.
Part 4 — Mapping vs setting. This is the key idea. Ask the class:

What happens if you put fill = "blue" inside aes()? Have them try it first. — The bars are pink-red and the legend says “blue”: ggplot treated “blue” as data (a column whose every value is the word “blue”) and gave it the first default color.

Part 5 — Scatter plots. With 6,451 rows, many points overlap — show size and alpha fixing that. When filtering inside the pipeline, point out the switch: %>% into ggplot(), then + between layers. In the TRY IT, emphasize that a flat trend line (“no relationship”) is a result too.
Part 6 — Box plots. Walk through the parts of the box (median, IQR, whiskers at 1.5 × IQR, outliers). Ask the class:

Why is the mean (diamond) above the median (line)? — The ages are right-skewed: a few older patients pull the mean up (female: median 11, mean 12.7; male: median 17, mean 19.5).

Mention geom_violin() as an alternative.
Part 7 — Labels and themes. Point out that a complete theme like theme_minimal() resets everything, so it must come before theme(legend.position = ...). base_size = 14 is handy for slides. Early finishers: ⭐ BONUS (fill by vaccinated; geom_violin()).

title: Instructor notes: Session 8
text:
Teaching notes by part
The motivating example. Keep returning to it: “Your manager wants an epidemic curve for every hospital, every week.” By the end, one loop does it.
Part 2 — Writing your first function. Show that a function only exists after you run the whole block — it then appears in the Variables pane. When you change a function, re-run the block, or R keeps using the old version. Point out that c_to_f() is vectorized because the maths inside is, so it works inside mutate(). The f_to_c(104.7) result (40.4) is the Fahrenheit temperature learners found in the measles data in Session 1.
Part 3 — Functions that use data. Point out that pct() replaces the round(mean(...) * 100, 1) learners wrote over and over in Session 5, and that paste("Weekly cases:", hospital) gives every plot the right title. In the TRY IT, watch for learners naming the argument district: then filter(district == district) compares the column with itself and keeps every row — no error, just the wrong answer (n = 1163 instead of 342). That’s why the argument is called district_name. The lesson page has this as a warning box.
Part 4 — if / else. Run fever_status(c(39.2, 36.9)) live so learners see the error “the condition has length > 1”: if asks one yes/no question. Then switch to the vectorized if_else() from Session 2. Present stop() input checks as where if really shines. (Both error chunks are deliberate; the lesson page shows the errors.)
Part 5 — for loops. Stress that inside a loop nothing prints automatically (print()), and that results need a container created before the loop. In the payoff loop, point out make_clean_names() turning “St. Mark’s Maternity Hospital” into st_marks_maternity_hospital and paste0() building the file name: six files, one loop — and next week you just re-run it. Have learners check the Explorer for the new files in outputs/. Remind them that mutate(), group_by() + summarise(), and across() already loop for them; a for loop is for repeating a whole task.
Part 6 — map() and walk(). Point out that a data frame is a list of columns, so map_dbl() runs once per column, and that ~ .x is the same shorthand they used with across() in Session 3. Loop or map()? Both are fine — tell learners to use the one they can read.
Wrap-up. Today: function(), arguments and defaults, if/else, stop(), if_else(), for loops, map(), map_dbl(), walk(). The big idea: write it once, run it many times — a function plus a loop (or walk()) turns an hour of copy-paste into one line you can re-run every week. Where to go next: R for Data Science (functions and iteration chapters) and The Epidemiologist R Handbook.

clean_names()

[10] "age_unit"          "wt_kg"             "ht_cm"            








TipOne step at a time



We build the clean data step by step. Each step takes the current version, changes one thing, and saves it back with <-:
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>% STEP()
If your object gets into a bad state, re-run from the first step (linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>% clean_names()). In Part 7 we put all the steps into one pipeline.








Important✏️ TRY IT (2 min): clean the measles column names

text:
Dates
as.Date() converts text or date-times to dates.

linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(
    date_of_infection = as.Date(date_of_infection),
    onset_date        = as.Date(onset_date),
    hospital_date     = as.Date(hospital_date),
    date_of_outcome   = as.Date(date_of_outcome)
  )

linelist_clean %>% select(date_of_infection:date_of_outcome) %>% glimpse()

Rows: 6,604
Columns: 4
$ date_of_infection <date> 2014-05-08, NA, NA, 2014-05-04, 2014-05-18, 2014-05…
$ onset_date        <date> 2014-05-13, 2014-05-13, 2014-05-16, 2014-05-18, 201…
$ hospital_date     <date> 2014-05-15, 2014-05-14, 2014-05-18, 2014-05-20, 201…
$ date_of_outcome   <date> NA, 2014-05-18, 2014-05-30, NA, 2014-05-29, 2014-05…








NoteDates written in other formats



as.Date() expects year-month-day ("2014-05-13"). For other formats, the lubridate package (part of the tidyverse) has functions named after the order: dmy("13/05/2014"), mdy("05/13/2014"), ymd("2014-05-13").

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Numbers stored as text
as.numeric() turns text like "56" into the number 56. Text that isn’t a number (like "unknown") becomes NA, and R warns you: “NAs introduced by coercion”. That warning is fine if you expected it.

linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age = as.numeric(age))

class(linelist_clean$age)

[1] "numeric"








WarningCommon mistakes




Forgetting the <- at the start: the result prints in the Console but isn’t saved.









Important✏️ TRY IT (3 min): fix the measles types



In measles_clean:

make report_date a date with as.Date()
make age_years a number with as.numeric(). Which values became NA?

✅ Check: summary(measles_clean$age_years) shows a maximum of 999. Suspicious!






NoteShow solution






measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    report_date = as.Date(report_date),
    age_years   = as.numeric(age_years)   # "unknown" becomes NA (the warning is expected)
  )

summary(measles_clean$age_years)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
   0.00    4.00    7.00   12.13   12.00  999.00      27 


The 27 "unknown" ages became NA — that is what the warning is about. A maximum age of 999 is not a real age; we fix it in the next part.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Ages in months → years
“If the unit is months, divide by 12; otherwise keep the age.”

linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age_years = if_else(age_unit == "months", age / 12, age))

linelist_clean %>%
  filter(age_unit == "months") %>%
  select(age, age_unit, age_years) %>%
  head()

  age age_unit age_years
1  24   months 2.0000000
2  NA   months        NA
3   7   months 0.5833333
4   7   months 0.5833333
5  24   months 2.0000000
6  24   months 2.0000000








Note🤔 Think about it: what would have happened in later analyses if we had skipped this step?





A 6-month-old baby would be counted as 6 years old. All 37 ages recorded in months would be too old, which would shift the age groups and the average age.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Impossible values → missing
Weights of zero or below are impossible. Instead of deleting the whole row (and losing the patient’s age, outcome, and dates), we replace only the bad value with NA.

linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(wt_kg = if_else(wt_kg <= 0, NA, wt_kg))

summary(linelist_clean$wt_kg)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
   1.00   41.00   55.00   52.99   66.00  111.00      34 








Important✏️ TRY IT (4 min): 999 and Fahrenheit



In measles_clean:

999 is a code for “unknown”: replace age_years of 999 with NA
temperatures above 45 were entered in Fahrenheit. Convert them: Celsius = (Fahrenheit − 32) × 5 / 9, rounded to 1 decimal with round(..., 1)

✅ Check: summary() shows age_years max 52 and temp_c max 40.9






NoteShow solution






measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    age_years = if_else(age_years == 999, NA, age_years),
    temp_c    = if_else(temp_c > 45, round((temp_c - 32) * 5 / 9, 1), temp_c)
  )

summary(measles_clean$age_years)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   8.796  12.000  52.000      31 

summary(measles_clean$temp_c)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  36.00   38.40   38.90   38.82   39.40   40.90 


The four 999s are now NA (31 missing ages in total), and the 27 Fahrenheit temperatures are now in °C, so every temperature is between 36 and 40.9.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
BMI
mutate() can calculate a new column from other columns.

linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(bmi = round(wt_kg / (ht_cm / 100)^2, 1))

summary(linelist_clean$bmi)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  10.90   24.60   32.10   48.09   49.88 1250.00      34 








Note🤔 Think about it: a BMI of 1,250?





That is impossible: the heights and weights don’t fit together. Set BMIs outside a plausible range (10–60) to NA.




linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(bmi = if_else(bmi < 10 | bmi > 60, NA, bmi))

summary(linelist_clean$bmi)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  10.90   23.20   28.70   30.58   36.50   60.00    1382 


About 1,400 BMIs are now NA, because many height and weight values in this teaching dataset are unrealistic. Setting only the bad value to NA (instead of filtering out those rows) keeps everything else we know about each patient.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Age groups

linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age_cat = case_when(
    age_years < 18 ~ "Under 18",
    age_years < 30 ~ "18-29",
    age_years < 40 ~ "30-39",
    age_years < 50 ~ "40-49",
    age_years < 60 ~ "50-59",
    age_years < 70 ~ "60-69",
    age_years < 80 ~ "70-79",
    age_years >= 80 ~ "80+"
  ))

linelist_clean %>% count(age_cat)

Because case_when() stops at the first TRUE line, age_years < 30 only catches ages 18–29 (younger ages were already caught by the line above).
count() lists the groups in alphabetical order (“18-29” before “Under 18”). In Session 5 you will learn how to put them in a sensible order with factors.






WarningCommon mistakes



Ending with TRUE ~ "80+" (or .default = "80+") puts every patient with a missing age into the 80+ group. Write the last condition out in full (age_years >= 80 ~ "80+") so missing ages stay NA.

“died” and “recovered” now match “Died” and “Recovered” (52 died, 1095 recovered, 68 missing). The 31 missing ages (the 27 “unknown” plus the four 999s) stay NA because the last condition is written out in full.

title: Session 2: Cleaning Your Data
text:
Save your work
export() is the opposite of import(). Save cleaned data to processed_data/ — never over the raw file.

export(linelist_clean, here("processed_data", "linelist_clean.rds"))

.rds is R’s own file format. It keeps everything exactly as it is in R — dates stay dates and missing values stay NA — so it’s the best choice for a file you will open in R again. (We compare .rds and .csv in Session 3.)
Session 3 starts from this file.






Important✏️ TRY IT (2 min): save the measles data



Save measles_clean as processed_data/measles_clean.rds. You need this file in Session 3!

Same pattern as for linelist_clean: export(DATA, here("FOLDER", "FILE_NAME.rds")). Session 3 starts by importing this file.











Tip⭐ Bonus




Rewrite all of your measles TRY ITs as one pipeline that starts from measles_raw (like Part 7). It should give the same result — see the solutions file.
Brought your own data? Fix the problems on your own problem list, then export() the clean version to processed_data/.

text:
One type per vector
If you mix types, R converts everything to the most flexible type — usually text. This is why a single “unknown” turned the whole age column into text in Session 1:

c(1, 2, "unknown")

[1] "1"       "2"       "unknown"

c(1, TRUE, FALSE)    # TRUE becomes 1, FALSE becomes 0

[1] 1 1 0

text:
Missing values spread
Any calculation with NA gives NA, unless you tell R to skip them:

mean(c(38, 39, NA))

[1] NA

mean(c(38, 39, NA), na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 38.5








Important✏️ TRY IT (3 min): types in the measles data



Use class() on measles$age_years, measles$vaccinated, and measles$report_date, and length() on measles$temp_c.
✅ Check: “numeric”, “character”, “Date”, and 1163

[1] "numeric"

class(measles$vaccinated)

[1] "character"

class(measles$report_date)

[1] "Date"

Ages are numbers, vaccination status is text, and the report date is a real date. The length is 1163 — one value per row, because a column is just a vector.

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Subsetting, and Reshaping

Comparisons are vectorized too
A comparison gives a logical vector, one TRUE/FALSE per element:

temps_c > 38

[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE


TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0, so:

sum() of a comparison counts the TRUEs
mean() of a comparison gives the proportion that are TRUE


sum(linelist$temp > 38, na.rm = TRUE)    # how many patients had temp above 38

[1] 4943

mean(linelist$temp > 38, na.rm = TRUE)   # what proportion

[1] 0.7846032

mean(linelist$fever == "yes")            # proportion with fever

[1] 0.7870098


You will use this trick again in Session 5: mean(fever == "yes") * 100 inside summarise() gives the percentage with fever in each group.

[1] 565

565 cases had a temperature of 39 °C or more, and 23.8% of cases were vaccinated. No na.rm = TRUE is needed here because temp_c has no missing values after cleaning.

WarningBase R and missing values




nrow(linelist[linelist$temp > 40, ])   # 244 rows?!

[1] 244

nrow(filter(linelist, temp > 40))     # 93 rows

[1] 93


Base R returns an extra row of NAs for every missing temperature (151 of them). filter() drops rows where the condition is NA. With base R, add & !is.na(temp), or just use filter():

nrow(linelist[linelist$temp > 40 & !is.na(linelist$temp), ])   # 93: fixed

[1] 93

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Subsetting, and Reshaping
text:
Base R vs tidyverse








Task
Base R
Tidyverse




Rows that meet a condition
df[df$age > 40, ]
filter(df, age > 40)


Some columns
df[, c("a", "b")]
select(df, a, b)


One column as a vector
df$a or df[["a"]]
pull(df, a)


First rows
df[1:5, ]
slice(df, 1:5) or head(df, 5)









WarningCommon mistakes




Forgetting the comma: df[1:3] picks columns 1–3, not rows!
Base R adds a row of NAs for every NA in the condition (see the box above). Add & !is.na(...), or use filter().









Important✏️ TRY IT (5 min): subsetting the measles data



With base R,

Show rows 1–5 of the patient_id and temp_c columns of measles
Find the mean temperature of children who died (outcome == "Died")
Count the cases aged 15 or older with nrow(measles[...]), then with filter(). Why are the answers different? Fix the base R version.

✅ Check: a) the first ID is MS-0931 b) 38.75 c) 225 vs 196 (29 missing ages)






NoteShow solution






# a)
measles[1:5, c("patient_id", "temp_c")]

  patient_id temp_c
1    MS-0931   38.3
2    MS-0113   38.4
3    MS-0975   39.3
4    MS-0297   38.0
5    MS-0159   38.9

# b)
mean(measles$temp_c[measles$outcome == "Died"])

[1] 38.754

# c)
nrow(measles[measles$age_years >= 15, ])

[1] 225

nrow(filter(measles, age_years >= 15))

[1] 196

nrow(measles[measles$age_years >= 15 & !is.na(measles$age_years), ])   # fixed

[1] 196


Base R gives 225 rows because it adds a row of NAs for each of the 29 cases with a missing age. Adding & !is.na(measles$age_years) gives 196, the same as filter().

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Subsetting, and Reshaping
text:
Tidy data
Data is tidy when:

Each variable is a column
Each observation is a row
Each value is a cell

The tidyverse works best on tidy data. But “observation” depends on your question. Our symptoms are in wide format — one column per symptom:

linelist %>% select(case_id, fever:vomit) %>% head(3)

  case_id   fever  chills   cough   aches   vomit
1  5fe599      no      no     yes      no     yes
2  8689b7 Unknown Unknown Unknown Unknown Unknown
3  11f8ea Unknown Unknown Unknown Unknown Unknown


To count or plot all symptoms together, we want long format: one row per patient per symptom.
crumbs: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Subsetting, and Reshaping

title: Session 4: Data Structures — Vectors, Subsetting, and Reshaping
text:
pivot_longer(): wide → long

symptoms_long <- linelist %>%
  select(case_id, fever:vomit) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = fever:vomit,   # the columns to stack
    names_to  = "symptom",     # new column for the old column NAMES
    values_to = "present"      # new column for the VALUES
  )

head(symptoms_long)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  case_id symptom present
  <chr>   <chr>   <chr>  
1 5fe599  fever   no     
2 5fe599  chills  no     
3 5fe599  cough   yes    
4 5fe599  aches   no     
5 5fe599  vomit   yes    
6 8689b7  fever   Unknown

nrow(symptoms_long)   # 6451 patients × 5 symptoms

[1] 32255


fever:vomit means “every column from fever to vomit”.
Now one count() answers “how many patients had each symptom?”:

symptom_counts <- symptoms_long %>%
  filter(present == "yes") %>%
  count(symptom)

symptom_counts

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  symptom     n
  <chr>   <int>
1 aches     604
2 chills   1209
3 cough    5347
4 fever    5077
5 vomit    3095


And it’s ready to plot (a preview of Session 6):

ggplot(symptom_counts, aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(symptom, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Patients reporting each symptom", x = "Number of patients", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()














Important✏️ TRY IT (5 min): measles symptoms long



Select patient_id, fever, and rash from measles, then pivot_longer() the two symptom columns. count() symptom and present.
Pattern: pivot_longer(cols = c(COLUMN_1, COLUMN_2), names_to = "symptom", values_to = "present")
✅ Check: 2326 rows (1163 × 2); fever yes 1064, rash yes 976






NoteShow solution






measles_symptoms <- measles %>%
  select(patient_id, fever, rash) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(fever, rash),
    names_to  = "symptom",
    values_to = "present"
  )

nrow(measles_symptoms)

[1] 2326

measles_symptoms %>% count(symptom, present)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  symptom present     n
  <chr>   <chr>   <int>
1 fever   no         99
2 fever   yes      1064
3 rash    no        187
4 rash    yes       976


Each of the 1163 cases now has two rows, one for fever and one for rash, so there are 2326 rows. One count() gives the yes/no totals for both symptoms.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Fixed colors
Inside geom_histogram(), fill is the inside color and color is the outline. A white outline separates the bars.

ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")














NoteColors in R



Use a name ("steelblue", "gray50") or a hex code ("#2a78d6"). Run colors() to see all 657 named colors.








Important✏️ TRY IT (3 min): measles ages



Make a histogram of measles age_years with binwidth = 1, a fill color, and a white outline. Which age has the most cases?
✅ Check: the tallest bar is at age 2 (about 100 cases). The warning about “removed rows” is the 29 missing ages: that’s fine.






NoteShow solution






ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")








The tallest bar is age 2 (102 cases), and most cases are ages 1–5. ggplot can’t draw the 29 rows with a missing age, so it drops them and tells you.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Add a trend line
geom_smooth() adds a trend line on top of the points. method = "lm" draws a straight line (linear model); se = FALSE hides the confidence band.

ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#eb6834")

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Filter right inside ggplot()
You can pipe data into ggplot(), so you can filter() first without making a new object:

linelist %>%
  filter(fever == "yes") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = wt_kg)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.3)








Notice the switch: %>% into ggplot(), then + between layers.






Important✏️ TRY IT (4 min): a scatter plot



For hospitalized patients only (filter(!is.na(days_in_hospital))), plot age_years (x) against days_in_hospital (y) with alpha, and add a trend line. Is there a relationship?
✅ Check: 427 hospitalized patients; the trend line is almost flat (no relationship)






NoteShow solution






measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(days_in_hospital)) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = age_years, y = days_in_hospital)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#eb6834")








The trend line is almost flat: older and younger patients stay in hospital about as long. “No relationship” is a result too!

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Clean it up
Remove the “Unknown” group, color the boxes, and drop the legend (the x-axis already names the groups):

linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Add the mean
stat_summary() calculates a statistic for each group and draws it. Here, the mean as a diamond:

linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")














Note🤔 Think about it: why is the mean (diamond) above the median (line)?





The ages are right-skewed: a few older patients pull the mean up. For example, the median age of female cases is 11 but the mean is 12.7.









Note



geom_violin() shows the full shape of each distribution. Try swapping it in for geom_boxplot().








Important✏️ TRY IT (4 min): a box plot



Make a box plot of days_in_hospital by vaccinated (hospitalized patients only), with the mean and no legend.
✅ Check: three boxes; the medians are 4–5 days for every group






NoteShow solution






measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(days_in_hospital)) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = vaccinated, y = days_in_hospital, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








The medians are 4 days (Yes) and 5 days (No, Unknown), and the means are all about 5: no clear difference in hospital stay by vaccination status. The boxes appear in the order you set with fct_relevel() in Part 1.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
text:
Themes
A theme changes the look of everything that isn’t data: background, grid lines, fonts. Try theme_minimal(), theme_classic(), theme_bw(), and theme_light().

ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution of cases",
    x     = "Age (years)",
    y     = "Number of cases"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)








base_size makes all the text bigger — useful for slides.






WarningOrder matters



A complete theme like theme_minimal() resets everything, so put it before theme(legend.position = ...) or your change will be overwritten.

title: Session 6: Plotting Basics with ggplot2
section: Save a plot as an object
text:
Save a plot as an object
A plot can be saved with <- and built on later:

age_plot <- ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")

age_plot +
  labs(title = "Age distribution of cases", x = "Age (years)", y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_minimal()














Important✏️ TRY IT (5 min): finish a plot



Finish one of your measles plots with a title, subtitle, axis labels, a caption, and a theme. Save it as my_plot.
✅ Check: typing my_plot in the Console shows your finished plot

my_plot <- ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = temp_c, fill = fever)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, color = "white") +
  labs(
    title    = "Temperature of measles cases",
    subtitle = "Patients with fever cluster around 39 °C",
    x        = "Temperature (°C)",
    y        = "Number of cases",
    fill     = "Fever",
    caption  = "Source: practice measles linelist"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

my_plot








This is one example — any measles plot works. fill = "Fever" inside labs() renames the legend title. Saving the plot as my_plot stores it in the Variables pane, and typing its name draws it.

title: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration
text:
Why write functions?
If you copy and paste code more than twice, write a function. Functions:

avoid copy-paste mistakes (change it once, fixed everywhere)
give a task a clear name (c_to_f() says what it does)
make your scripts shorter and easier to read
crumbs: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration

title: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration
text:
The shape of a function

c_to_f <- function(temp_c) {
  temp_c * 9 / 5 + 32
}


c_to_f is the name — you save a function with <- like any object. Run the whole block to create it; then it appears in the Variables pane
temp_c is the argument — the input. Inside the function, it is whatever value you pass in
The code between { } is the body
The function returns the result of its last line


c_to_f(38)

[1] 100.4

c_to_f(c(36.8, 38.5, 40.1))   # it's vectorized, because the maths inside is

[1]  98.24 101.30 104.18


Because it’s vectorized, it works on a whole column inside mutate():

linelist %>%
  mutate(temp_f = c_to_f(temp)) %>%
  select(case_id, temp, temp_f) %>%
  head(3)

  case_id temp temp_f
1  5fe599 36.8  98.24
2  8689b7 36.9  98.42
3  11f8ea 36.9  98.42

title: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration
text:
Default values
Give an argument a default with =. You can change it, but you don’t have to:

c_to_f <- function(temp_c, digits = 1) {
  round(temp_c * 9 / 5 + 32, digits)
}

c_to_f(38.37)              # uses digits = 1

[1] 101.1

c_to_f(38.37, digits = 0)  # overrides it

[1] 101








WarningCommon mistakes




Changing the function but not re-running the block: R still uses the old version.









Important✏️ TRY IT (4 min): Fahrenheit to Celsius



Write f_to_c(temp_f) that converts Fahrenheit to Celsius: (temp_f - 32) * 5 / 9, rounded to 1 decimal. Test it on 98.6 and 104.7.
✅ Check: f_to_c(98.6) is 37 and f_to_c(104.7) is 40.4






NoteShow solution






f_to_c <- function(temp_f) {
  round((temp_f - 32) * 5 / 9, 1)
}

f_to_c(98.6)

[1] 37

f_to_c(104.7)

[1] 40.4


104.7 °F is 40.4 °C — the Fahrenheit temperature you found in the measles data in Session 1!

A function that takes a data frame

    filter(hospital_name == hospital) %>%
    summarise(
      n         = n(),
      pct_death = pct(outcome == "Death")
    )

hospital_summary(linelist, "Military Hospital")

title: Session 8: Programming — Functions, if/else, Loops, and Iteration
section: A function that makes a plot
text:
A function that makes a plot

make_epicurve <- function(data, hospital) {
  data %>%
    filter(hospital_name == hospital, onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = onset_date)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Weekly cases:", hospital),
      x     = "Week of onset",
      y     = "Number of cases"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

make_epicurve(linelist, "Military Hospital")








paste("Weekly cases:", hospital) builds the title from the argument, so every plot gets the right title.






WarningCommon mistake: name the argument district_name, not district



Don’t give an argument the same name as a column! In
function(data, district) { data %>% filter(district == district) }
R compares the district column with itself, so every row is kept — no error, just the wrong answer. Name the argument district_name instead: filter(district == district_name).








Important✏️ TRY IT (6 min): measles functions




Write rate_per_10k(cases, population) that returns cases / population * 10000, rounded to 1 decimal. Use it in mutate() after count(district, population).
Write district_summary(data, district_name) that returns the number of cases and the percentage vaccinated (use your pct() function!) for one district.

✅ Check: a) East is 22.8 b) district_summary(measles, "North") gives n 342, 25.7%






NoteShow solution






# a)
rate_per_10k <- function(cases, population) {
  round(cases / population * 10000, 1)
}

measles %>%
  count(district, population) %>%
  mutate(rate = rate_per_10k(n, population)) %>%
  arrange(desc(rate))

  district population   n rate
1     East      98000 223 22.8
2     West      76500 170 22.2
3    South     142000 284 20.0
4    North     185000 342 18.5
5  Central     210000 110  5.2
6  Unknown         NA  34   NA

# b)
district_summary <- function(data, district_name) {
  data %>%
    filter(district == district_name) %>%
    summarise(
      n              = n(),
      pct_vaccinated = pct(vaccinated == "Yes")
    )
}

district_summary(measles, "North")

    n pct_vaccinated
1 342           25.7


East has the highest rate, 22.8 cases per 10,000. North has 342 cases, and 25.7% of them were vaccinated. Because the argument is called district_name, filter(district == district_name) keeps only North.

section: The payoff: one epidemic curve per hospital
text:
The payoff: one epidemic curve per hospital

for (h in hospitals) {
  p <- make_epicurve(linelist, h)
  file_name <- paste0("epicurve_", make_clean_names(h), ".png")
  ggsave(here("outputs", file_name), plot = p, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
}


make_clean_names() (janitor) turns “St. Mark’s Maternity Hospital” into st_marks_maternity_hospital — safe for a file name
paste0() glues the pieces with no spaces into epicurve_st_marks_maternity_hospital.png
Six files, one loop. Next week, re-run it with the new data — check the Explorer to see the new files in outputs/







NoteYou’ve already been looping



mutate(), summarise() with group_by(), and across() all repeat work for you. In R, reach for those first; write a loop when you need to repeat a whole task, like making and saving a plot.








Important✏️ TRY IT (6 min): one epicurve per district



Write make_measles_epicurve(data, district_name) for weekly cases by report_date in one district. Then loop over the five districts (not “Unknown”) and save each plot to outputs/ as measles_central.png, measles_east.png, …
✅ Check: five new .png files in the outputs folder






NoteShow solution






make_measles_epicurve <- function(data, district_name) {
  data %>%
    filter(district == district_name, !is.na(report_date)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = report_date)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Weekly measles cases:", district_name),
      x     = "Week of report",
      y     = "Number of cases"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

districts <- c("Central", "East", "North", "South", "West")

for (d in districts) {
  p <- make_measles_epicurve(measles, d)
  file_name <- paste0("measles_", make_clean_names(d), ".png")
  ggsave(here("outputs", file_name), plot = p, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
}

The loop creates five files in outputs/: measles_central.png, measles_east.png, measles_north.png, measles_south.png, and measles_west.png. Again, the argument is district_name, not district.

title: Setup
text:
Before Session 1 (one-time setup)

Install R (version 4.2 or newer) from CRAN.
Install Positron (free) from Posit. Positron is the program you write and run R code in. Install R first (step 1), then Positron.
Download the workshop folder: download the ZIP file and unzip it somewhere easy to find (Documents, not Downloads). This one download has everything for all eight sessions.
Open the workshop folder in Positron: open Positron, choose File → Open Folder…, select the unzipped CWML-R-Hands-on-Workshop-Series folder, and click Open. If Positron asks whether you trust the authors of the files, click Yes.

The workshop files appear in the Explorer on the left.
An R Console starts at the bottom. If it doesn’t, click the interpreter button in the top-right corner and choose R.

Install the packages. Copy this into the Console (bottom) and press Enter:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here", "rio", "janitor", "skimr", "gtsummary", "flextable", "scales"))
It can take 5–10 minutes. If you see errors about compilers, see Troubleshooting.
Test it. Copy this into the Console and press Enter:
library(tidyverse); library(here); library(rio); library(janitor); library(skimr); library(gtsummary); library(flextable)
nrow(import(here("raw_data", "measles_raw.csv")))







Tip✅ You’re ready if it prints [1] 1215



Red messages that don’t start with “Error” are normal. If you see an error, contact the instructor before the session.








NoteAlready use RStudio?



That works too. Install the packages the same way, and open the workshop by double-clicking CWML-R-Hands-on-Workshop-Series.Rproj instead of using Open Folder. Everything else in the workshop is the same. (In RStudio, Positron’s Variables pane is called Environment, and the Explorer is the Files pane.)
